title: Show HN: FELF – AppImage-like single binaries without FUSE, root, or a runtime
text:
Hello HN!

I've always had a bad time redistributing programs that use shared libraries, AppImage in my opinion does too much, and a container is an overkill - not always integrates smoothly.

I've moved to nix since long ago, but redistributing between nix and other distros or vice versa it's still a pain in the ass, more so if you want to run an alien app in nix or a nix app without the package manger in any other distro.

For that, with the help of Claude, I've implemented a format that deduces at pack-time all the shared libraries a program needs, puts them, together with its own glibc and a patched dynamic linker into a single executable.

This means that you don't actually need a runtime nor any special capability, it can run inside a FROM SCRATCH docker, alpine linux etc... And it also supports coreutils-like multiple programs accessible via symlinks, so it is a good fit for that purpose.

You can just use:

> felf pack $(which git) --output git.felf

and you'll have already a git binary that works everywhere, no matter which distro you are building this from. This only packs the binary and their dependencies.

Essentially, the effect is similar as if you LD_PRELOAD's all the libraries that it requires.

In the end, we have been fighting these demons since long long ago, chroots/docker/appimage/flatpack/nix etc...

So this xkcd applies: https://xkcd.com/927/

I'm happy to share the project, I hope it inspires new discoveries/tools in this regard!

title: Why Agile Often Fails
text:
To be honest, I've always looked down on Agile and such methodologies, it's so hard to be fair when you've been bombarded with buzzwords for a long time. Even terms like "iterative" or "incremental" feel like buzzwords to me - even though they are very useful ideas. It felt like boring management stuff. But it turned out Agile is pretty good, but how people implement can differ, and it can go wrong.

Same goes for teaching best practices, some teachers like to follow rubrics: "top 10 things to do as a teacher". But often it fails and it turns students off because the teacher isn't focusing on the values behind the practices, they just implement them mindlessly. For example you see many teachers starting a lecture (in classroom or online course) by stating the objectives of the lecture. The problem is that they treat it as an item on their checklist and it often ends up being boring and soulless and you just feel like skipping it.

In my country we have an old wisdom that is loosely translated as: "judging a thing is a reflection of one's perception of it."

And how we perceive something can affect how motivated we are. For example, two people can perceive studying differently, and hence it can change how much they do it. It's part of being a human. Ideas can have a huge impact on our emotions and actions. The problem with many meetings is that not everyone in the team sees the value in them. Devs for instance often find meetings annoying and take a lot of time that could have been used for "real work" and build software. They perceive meetings as a chore, they think of it as a tool for the PM, management stuff - the PM wants to see if things are going well and if it's according to the plan. so the devs will probably speak as little as possible and just get it done to go back to "real work". - which sadly reduces the meeting's value. They think of it as a status sync. And that's how most stand up meetings are honestly. No wonder many people hate them.

But it doesn't have to be that way, if you can show your team that it can actually be useful for them, by actually designing useful meetings: if the meeting becomes a planning tool for everyone, a meeting that makes sure everyone is taking good decisions (and not just following the plan), not just a mere status sync. Devs might suddenly find it useful. If the devs start to think of it as a way to understand how the project is going and coming up with ways that make everyone work better. Suddenly it becomes important to them.

Yet changing someone's mindset about something is not easy or a simple process. And it's not just about throwing buzzwords or -ities. In fact even a term like "mindset" and "motivation" can be a turnoff to many people - including me. Human beings are complex, it's not a simple equation, thoughts affect emotions and behaviors, and behaviors will affect the thoughts again. And it's not as simple as changing how you perceive something, if something is truly useless no matter how one tries to think of it positively it would shatter when it faces the real world.

One final important idea is that we often try to seek perfection. As if we need to be passionate about everything! People don't need to love everything they do. It's okay if the meeting is a bit boring, it can have some value to the PM nevertheless. But we can do better.

title: Show HN: Velork – Design and Code, Together
text:
Hi HN! :)

I’ve been working as a fullstack freelancer for over 4 years now. I always wanted some kind of IDE where I could take designs, turn them into code, and not be restricted to using auto layout and all that stuff.

Back at the beginning of 2020, before LLMs and AI were a thing, I was sitting with a friend of mine trying to figure out how to take a design, even one built with absolute values, and turn it into a working web app. I tried and failed :(

Today I’m launching Velork! It’s meant to be the IDE for everything frontend. You can design UIs, work in 3D, add motion, share your designs, and convert them into actual code with your favorite stack in just one click.

It also works with your current subscription, so you can bring Claude, Codex & more.

To help you get a feel for it, we’re giving away 2,000 free AI credits to every new user :)

I’m happy to answer anything about how it works under the hood. I’m also curious what you’d want an “IDE for everything frontend” to do that current tools don’t!

title: Show HN: Recalc – Spreadsheet where cells can be Claude Code or Codex terminals
text:
I built this because it was useful for me when building evals/benchmarks, and I decided to put it up for free for others. The goal was quite simple, make it easy to use a lead claude code / codex session in a panel on the side, while allowing every cell to also be a terminal session running claude/codex, and make it possible to continue a session in an actual terminal window if I needed to. They can all talk to each other using cells on the grid, named cells, or the MCP server that effectively glues the app together. I also found it useful for managing context within related but disparate sessions.

My real benchmark runs with recalc are internal to my startup, so to demonstrate some of the functionality I built a small FDA Bench with the tool (obtain and put together dossier's of FDA submissions, and see if a harnessed Claude could have accurately predicted pass/fail): https://github.com/sshah03/recalc#a-model-benchmark

It is still very much a work in progress, but given the versatility of spreadsheet apps, wanted to see how others see themselves using it and what doesn't exist that would be useful to them. Currently runs locally on macs, linux as well but that's less tested, and Windows hasn't been tested at all so that'll come in the future.

title: Show HN: Loop – your coding agents, from your phone
text:
Loop is a mobile-first companion workspace for the coding harnesses you already run. It aggregates results from your harnesses into a continuous feed that is easy to navigate and organize from your phone. I spent several months holding my newborn in one hand and trying to talk to agents one-handed on my phone. Every mobile UI is still based around chat, and it doesn’t scale on mobile, let alone one-handed!

So I built Loop: a feed of the work your coding agents do. It’s built around agent results, not chats. You can scroll your history, get notified, save outputs, search and return to conversations later. The goal is to make interacting with agents via your phone feel familiar and intuitive based on the mobile UX we’ve all come to expect.

Loop runs on your own computer — no account, no server, no app store — and pairs with your phone with one QR scan. It wraps the agents you already use (Codex, Claude Code, Pi, OpenCode, Antigravity, Muse Code, Grok Build, or any ACP agent), each keeping its own context, tools, sign-in and billing — local models through Pi or OpenCode work too.

Apache-2.0, TypeScript, SQLite. I'd love feedback from anyone else who builds from a phone.

title: Re: Why I will not be using LLMs in my coding...
text:
It's not all black and white.

Do I write less and less code myself? Yes. Do I read less and less code? Maybe. Does it always matter? No. Sometimes, the agent writes code in a project or section of code that is sensitive and deserves a thorough review. Sometimes, it's in a tool that you would never have had the time to write if you didn't have an agent. Or it can be in a project that is so well covered by TDD that you can be confident that it won't break. There could be performance regressions or duplication / code creep, but once you realize it, you can ask an agent to simplify the code and find ways to prevent that from happening again.

There are cleanup / technical-debt-reduction tasks that I thought would never be done in my lifetime due to lack of time and other priorities. But now, I'm blasting through them with Claude. I cannot imagine the lack of productivity I would suffer if deprived from an agent.

That said, I agree with most points the author makes. It becomes harder to grok the code, just as it becomes hard to navigate without GPS navigation once you are used to it. It is maybe necessary to force oneself to do a development task once in a while without the help of an agent in order to stay sharp.

But stop using LLMs? that sounds counterproductive.

title: Re: JIT bitmap text rendering for microcontrollers...
text:
Related: for a project I needed readable vector fonts in as few bytes as possible. Had to handle full Unicode and any font face.

Setting Claude on the challenge and giving some pointers (use a set of ANS coders! Be lossy as long as there are no errors when rendered!), I was amazed that a typical font can be rendered in just ~40 bytes per used character.

It saddens me that despite this, plenty of websites ship hundreds of kilobytes of custom fonts!

title: Re: Llama-modchip: 284B DeepSeek on 64GB RAM, no GPU...
text:
The floor for a functional local AI system keeps getting lower, dispite ram and GPU prices continuing to go up. An E5 workstation with lots of threads, $300 of RAM and at least $100 of GPU gets you something that can do >100tok/s+ prompt processing, and ~20tok/s output with Qwen3.8-flash-next:IQ3_S. Toss a $500 GPU in there, and it goes from barely usable to pleasingly performant. For less than $800 you have something that holds its own with where the SOTA was less than a year ago.

I don't see how anyone justifies a claude subscription. Do you want to rent the tools you use to making a living from the people who are trying to automate away your job?
